# Introduction to marketing and industrial marketing

Campus Tees prints shirts for student clubs. Use this business in each example.

## Marketing, needs, wants and demands

**Lecture slides 2–5. Exact marketing definition:**

> A social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating and exchanging products and value with others.

**Plain English:** find out what people need. Offer something useful in exchange for money or other value.

| Term | Exact lecture wording | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Need | A state of felt deprivation. | A club needs its team to feel united. |
| Want | The form that a human need takes as shaped by culture and individual personality. | The club wants orange shirts with its logo. |
| Demand | Human wants that are backed by purchasing power. | The club wants 100 shirts and can pay for them. |

**Plain English:** a need is something missing. A want is the chosen solution. Demand means the buyer can pay.

[diagram:needs]

## Industrial marketing and derived demand

**Slide 6. Exact definition:**

> Marketing of goods and services to individuals and organizations for purposes other than personal consumption

**Plain English:** sell to an organisation for its work, rather than for someone's private use.

**Campus Tees:** selling volunteer shirts to a club is a business purchase. Selling one shirt for personal use is a consumer purchase.

**Derived demand:** a business buys inputs because its customers need the final product. More club orders lead Campus Tees to buy more blank shirts.

**Slide 7:** business markets often have fewer, larger buyers. Buyers may check technical details, involve several people and keep long supplier relationships.

## Segmentation, targeting and positioning

**Slide 8. Exact definition of segmentation:**

> To divide a market into distinct groups of buyers with different needs, characteristics or behaviors, who might require separate products or marketing mixes.

**Plain English:** put buyers with similar needs into useful groups.

**Slide 9: six steps.**

| Step | What Campus Tees does |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Identify segmentation bases. | Group buyers by order size, use or delivery needs. |
| 2. Develop segment profiles. | Describe clubs, sports teams and local firms. |
| 3. Measure segment attractiveness. | Compare demand, likely profit and the cost of serving each group. |
| 4. Select target segments. | Choose clubs ordering 100–500 shirts. |
| 5. Develop positioning. | Be known for reliable event shirts and simple ordering. |
| 6. Develop the marketing mix. | Offer suitable shirts, prices, ordering channels and promotion. |

[diagram:stp]

**Keep the difference clear:** segmentation finds the groups. Targeting chooses which groups to serve. Positioning explains why those buyers should choose the firm.

The marketing mix covers **product, price, place and promotion**. Campus Tees must have enough shirts and printing time to keep its delivery promise.

## Reading for this lecture

No separate paper is named in these lecture slides. Use the original slides and the module reading list linked above.


# SCM and strategy fundamentals

## Supply chain management and flows

**Slide 2, Christopher (2011). Exact definition:**

> The management of upstream and downstream relationships with suppliers and customers in order to deliver superior customer value at less cost to the supply chain as a whole.

**Plain English:** help suppliers and customers work together. Give customers better value while keeping the whole chain's cost low.

**Campus Tees:** a cheap shirt is a poor choice if late delivery makes the club miss its event.

**Slides 4 and 8:** goods usually move towards the customer. Payments usually move towards suppliers. Orders, forecasts and delivery information move both ways. Returns move goods back.

[diagram:supply]

## Strategy, customer value and the value chain

**Slides 5–7:** ask where the firm is now, where it wants to be, and how it will get there.

Ohmae's three Cs are **customer, company and competitor**. Campus Tees must understand club needs, its own skills and other printers' offers.

Porter's primary activities are **inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service**. Support activities are **infrastructure, human resources, technology and procurement**.

**Plain English:** look at every part of the work. Ask how each part adds value or cost.

[diagram:valuechain]

## Integration and Christopher's four Rs

**Slide 9:** integration has four stages: separate departments; joined functions; the whole firm working together; the firm working with suppliers and customers.

**Campus Tees:** sales shares confirmed orders with printing. The shirt supplier also sees the delivery plan.

[diagram:integration]

| Four Rs: slides 10–11 | Simple meaning | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Responsiveness | Respond to a change quickly. | Change the print plan after a club updates its order. |
| Reliability | Do what was promised. | Deliver the correct shirts on Friday. |
| Resilience | Keep working and recover after a problem. | Use a qualified backup supplier. |
| Relationships | Work well with other firms. | Solve delivery problems with the wholesaler. |

**Christopher reading:** customer value and total chain cost belong together. A saving in purchasing can create extra stock, waste or delivery costs elsewhere.

## Barney: resources and sustained advantage

**Reading: Barney (1991), pp. 101–102.** Resources include equipment, people, knowledge and ways of working. **Resource heterogeneity** means firms have different resources. **Imperfect resource mobility** means some resources cannot move easily between firms.

**Exact definition of sustained competitive advantage:**

> A firm is said to have a sustained competitive advantage when it is implementing a value creating strategy not simultaneously being implemented by any current or potential competitors and when these other firms are unable to duplicate the benefits of this strategy.

**Plain English:** the firm creates value in a way rivals do not use. Rivals also cannot copy the benefits.

| VRIN test | Simple question | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Valuable | Does it help the firm meet a need or deal with a threat? | A reliable routine helps meet event deadlines. |
| Rare | Do few rivals have it? | Few printers have the same trusted club network. |
| Imperfectly imitable | Is it hard to copy? | Years of trust and shared experience are hard to buy. |
| Non-substitutable | Is there no easy alternative that gives the same benefit? | Check whether another system can give equal service. |

[diagram:vrin]

Copying may be hard because of **history**, **causal ambiguity** or **social complexity**. These mean a unique past, unclear reasons for success, or complex human relationships. A printer anyone can buy is unlikely to pass all four tests. Sustained does not mean forever.

## Other supply chain terms to know

These terms also appear in the supplied exam papers.

**Bullwhip:** small changes in customer sales cause larger changes in orders upstream. Share real sales data and agree how to order stock.

**SCOR:** a common model for describing, measuring and improving supply chain work. Classic names are Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return and Enable. The Digital Standard uses Orchestrate, Plan, Order, Source, Transform, Fulfill and Return. Do not mix the versions.

**Risk:** a supplier failure or wrong demand forecast can stop work. Qualified alternatives, useful buffers and shared plans can reduce the damage. They also cost money.

**Sustainability:** consider the environment, people and long-term business costs across the chain. Campus Tees can reduce unsold prints and work with suppliers to improve working conditions.


# Purchasing and supply management

## Purchasing and its financial effect

**Slide 3, van Weele (2005:12). Exact definition:**

> The management of the company’s external resources in such a way that the supply of all goods, services, capabilities and knowledge which are necessary for running, maintaining and managing the company’s primary and support activities is secured at the most favourable conditions.

**Plain English:** get the outside goods, services and skills the business needs, on suitable terms. Price is only one part.

**Slide 4: DuPont example.** Sales are 100, purchases 60, other costs 38 and assets 20. Profit is 2. ROI is 2/20 = **10%**.

A 5% saving on purchases reduces them to 57. Profit becomes 5 and ROI becomes **25%**, if everything else stays the same.

**Campus Tees:** cheaper blanks help only if extra defects or late deliveries do not remove the saving.

## Gadde and Håkansson: three strategic choices

**Slide 5 and the assigned paper.**

| Issue | Simple question | Campus Tees example and limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Make or buy: scope of supply | Which work should we do ourselves? | Keep key printing skills inside; buy outside transport. Buying can add skills but also dependence. |
| Supplier-base structure | How many suppliers, and how are they linked? | Use a main wholesaler and a qualified backup. More suppliers also need more checking. |
| Nature of relationships | How closely should we work with suppliers? | Share plans for important shirts. Close work takes time and can make switching harder. |

**From the paper:** close relationships can reduce admin and production costs. This is **rationalisation**. They can also support **technical development**, such as testing a better fabric together.

The choices affect each other. Buying more outside work can make supplier skills and close planning more important.

**Single sourcing:** use one supplier for a need. **Multiple sourcing:** use several. **Parallel sourcing:** use different suppliers for different product lines while keeping close relationships within each line.

## Core competence and outsourcing

**Slide 6: core competence** combines skills and resources that help the firm compete. It should open several markets, add customer benefit and be hard to copy.

**Campus Tees:** knowing how to handle custom club orders may matter more than owning a delivery van.

**Slide 7. Exact outsourcing definition:**

> Complete transfer of a business process to an independent external organization

**Plain English:** another firm takes over a business process.

**Slides 8–12:** outsourcing can lower costs, provide skills and free time for core work. Hidden costs include quality problems, supplier management, internal coordination and setting up the new arrangement.

## Kraljic's purchasing matrix

**Slides 13–14 and Kraljic (1983).** The axes are **profit impact** and **supply risk**.

| Category | Impact / risk | Main action | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Routine / non-critical | Low / low | Simplify buying. | Standard office paper. |
| Leverage | High / low | Compare qualified offers and use buying volume. | Common blanks bought in large amounts. |
| Bottleneck | Low / high | Protect supply; consider a suitable buffer. | A low-cost spare from one supplier. |
| Strategic | High / high | Plan closely and manage a long-term relationship. | A special fabric central to the main product. |

[diagram:kraljic]

The lecture examples are office supplies, raw materials, flavours and engines. The category depends on the buying situation. Price alone does not decide it.

**From Kraljic's paper:** use four steps: **classification, market analysis, strategic positioning and action plans**. Compare buyer strength with supply-market strength. Possible directions include exploit, balance or diversify. Turn the analysis into choices about suppliers, stock and contracts.

[lab:kraljic]


# Inventory management

## Inventory and costs

Inventory is stock kept for later use or sale. Campus Tees holds blank shirts, work being printed and finished orders. Stock helps meet demand, but uses cash and storage space.

**Slides 3–5: three different cost questions.**

| Type | Simple meaning | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed / variable | Does the total change with output? | Rent stays fixed within a range. More shirts use more fabric. |
| Direct / indirect | Can the cost be linked to this order? | Blanks belong to one order. Shared office costs do not. |
| Engineered / discretionary | Is cost linked to the work, or chosen by managers? | Material use has a clear link to output. Managers choose a training budget. |

A direct cost can be fixed. A shared cost can vary. Fixed rent may rise when another room is needed.

## Break-even: how many shirts cover the costs?

**Slide 6.** Let F be fixed cost, p price per shirt, v variable cost per shirt and q shirts sold.

**Profit = (p − v) × q − F. Break-even quantity = F / (p − v).**

Campus Tees has F = €1,200, p = €15 and v = €9. Each shirt provides €6 towards fixed costs. Break-even is **1,200 / 6 = 200 shirts**. At 300 shirts, profit is **€600**.

The model assumes a steady price and unit cost, with fixed costs unchanged. Price must be above variable cost.

[lab:breakeven]

## Reorder point and safety stock

**Slide 7. Exact rule:**

> Re-order Point = demand during lead time + safety stock

**Plain English:** order before stock runs out. Cover the wait for delivery and keep a buffer.

**ROP = d × L + SS.** Daily demand d = 40 shirts, lead time L = 5 days, safety stock SS = 60. **ROP = 40 × 5 + 60 = 260 shirts.**

Safety stock protects against higher demand or late supply. The needed buffer depends on service goals and demand or lead-time changes. Better data helps, but cannot supply a missing shirt.

[diagram:reorder]

[lab:reorder]

## EOQ: how much should we order?

**From the glossary:** EOQ balances ordering cost and stockholding cost.

**Q* = √(2DK/h).** D is annual demand; K is cost per order; h is holding cost per unit per year.

For D = 12,000, K = €30 and h = €2, **EOQ = 600 shirts**. This means 20 orders per year and 300 shirts of average cycle stock. Annual ordering and holding costs are €600 each.

The basic model assumes steady demand, a fixed unit price, known lead time and complete deliveries. **EOQ means how much. ROP means when.** Keep time units the same.

[lab:eoq]

## Stock tools and systems

**Slides 8–9 and the glossary.** JIT aims to bring materials close to the time they are needed. It needs reliable quality, information and suppliers.

**ABC** gives more attention to items with high annual usage value. **FIFO** uses the oldest cost first; **LIFO** uses the newest cost first. Ten shirts at €2, then ten at €3: selling ten gives FIFO cost €20 or LIFO cost €30.

**MPS** plans finished output. **MRP** plans required materials. **ERP** joins business data. **WMS** manages warehouse work. **SKU** identifies a stock variant. **VMI** gives the supplier an agreed role in checking and refilling stock. See the short glossary for all 25 terms.

## Recommended inventory paper

**Panigrahi, Shrivastava and Nudurupati (2024): abstract only.** The full paper was not uploaded. The publisher's abstract says small firms need suitable stock methods, technology and staff knowledge. These can affect business performance.

**Campus Tees example:** a stock system helps only if staff enter correct shirt sizes and understand when to reorder. This is our example, not a case from the paper.


# Operations management

## Transformation and quality

**Slides 3–6:** operations change inputs into outputs that meet customer needs. A process contains smaller processes and activities.

**Campus Tees:** blank shirts, ink and staff time become printed club shirts.

**Slide 6. TQM definition (spelling corrected):**

> An organisation-wide effort to work with quality and continuous improvement (Kaizen)

**Plain English:** everyone helps prevent errors and improve the work. **Kaizen** means ongoing improvement. **BPR** means a major redesign of a business process. **Six Sigma** uses data to reduce defects and variation.

**Campus Tees:** fixing an artwork checklist is a small improvement. Replacing the whole order process is BPR.

[diagram:transformation]

## Seven wastes: MUDA

**Slide 7.**

| Waste | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- |
| Overproduction | Print more club designs than customers ordered. |
| Defects | Print the wrong logo. |
| Inventory | Keep too many unsold shirts. |
| Motion | Staff walk around looking for tools. |
| Overprocessing | Enter the same order twice. |
| Transporting | Move boxes between rooms without a need. |
| Waiting | Leave an order waiting for artwork approval. |

## P-time, D-time and the decoupling point

**Slide 8. Exact definitions:**

> P-Time is the production lead time

> D-Time is the time that the customer is willing to wait

> CODP – Customer Order Decoupling Point, defined as the point where the product is linked to a specific order

**Plain English:** P-time is the work's full lead time. D-time is the buyer's allowed wait. The CODP is where work becomes tied to one real order.

**Campus Tees:** supply takes 5 days, printing 2, delivery 1: P-time is 8 days. A club accepts 3 days. Hold common blanks before the order; print after the club confirms its logo.

[diagram:ptime]

## Lean, agile and leagile: Naylor, Naim and Berry

**Assigned paper, p. 108. Exact definitions:**

> Leanness means developing a value stream to eliminate all waste, including time, and to ensure a level schedule.

> Agility means using market knowledge and a virtual corporation to exploit profitable opportunities in a volatile market place.

**Plain English:** lean removes waste and keeps work steady. Agile uses customer information and flexible partners to respond to change. Lean often focuses on low cost; agile often focuses on quick service when demand changes.

**Leagile** combines them. Campus Tees buys common blanks in a steady, low-waste flow. After the CODP, it prints the confirmed design quickly. Both sides need good information and reliable processes.

[diagram:leagile]

**Slide 10. Exact postponement definition:**

> Postponement is a business strategy which maximizes possible benefit and minimizes risk by delaying further investment into a product or service until the last possible moment

**Plain English:** wait for better information before making a product specific. Still meet the promised date.

**From the paper:** keep common parts ready, then finish the required version later. This can reduce wrong finished stock. It needs enough finishing time and capacity.

## Match the method to demand and lead time

**Slide 11:** predictable demand with long lead time suits lean planning. Predictable demand with short lead time suits regular Kanban refills. Unpredictable demand with short lead time suits agile response. Unpredictable demand with long lead time can suit postponement.

## Reduce wasted time and find causes

**Slides 12–16:** a time-based map separates work time from waiting. A cause-and-effect diagram lists possible causes under people, machines, materials and methods. Check the causes with evidence.

**Campus Tees:** earlier artwork approval reduces waiting. A clear size check reduces wrong prints. Less waiting and rework can reduce stock, equipment needs and quality costs. Removing checks without controlling quality can create more defects.

[diagram:timeprocess]

[diagram:fishbone]


# Industrial networks

## Buy, make and work closely together

**Slide 3:** ownership and close cooperation are different choices.

| Form | Simple meaning | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classical market contracting | Buy from an independent firm. | Choose a courier for one delivery. |
| Quasi-vertical integration | Separate firms share some work, costs or risks. | Develop a delivery process with a long-term supplier. |
| Vertical integration | Own the activity. | Run an internal printing and delivery team. |

A firm can work closely with a supplier without owning it.

## IMP interaction model

**Slides 4–5:** repeated exchanges help firms learn about each other and reduce uncertainty.

The model includes **product/service, information, financial and social exchanges**. It also considers the firms and people involved, their relationship's atmosphere and the wider environment.

**Plain English:** what happens depends on the work, the people, their trust and the situation around them.

**Campus Tees:** the wholesaler learns the printer's size codes. Both firms agree on an order deadline. Their routines become linked. This helps delivery, but can make switching suppliers harder.

[diagram:interaction]

## ARA: three connected parts

**Slide 6. Keep the model's exact labels.**

| Part | Relationship link | Simple meaning and Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actors | Actor bonds | Who is involved: the printer and wholesaler build trust. |
| Resources | Resource ties | What they use: shirt fabric and print settings are adapted to fit. |
| Activities | Activity links | What they do: dispatch and printing schedules are joined. |

[diagram:ara]

The parts affect each other. Trust can support a fabric trial. The new fabric then changes printing and delivery work.

## Ford and Mouzas: business networking

**Assigned paper, p. 436. Exact definition:**

> Business networking is the conscious problem-driven attempts of one or more business actors to change or develop some aspect(s) of the substance of interaction in relationships in which they and others are involved.

**Plain English:** firms try to change connected business relationships to solve a problem.

**Campus Tees:** late deliveries lead the printer, wholesaler and courier to agree on a new handover time. Networking is more than meeting people.

## Three levels and network pictures

**From Ford and Mouzas.** Do not confuse these levels with ARA's three parts.

| Level | Simple meaning | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relationship | One direct relationship. | Printer and wholesaler. |
| Small world | Known links around the firm. | The wholesaler's link to a shirt maker. |
| Wider world | More distant actors and changes. | New industry rules that affect several firms. |

[diagram:networklevels]

A **network picture** is how an actor understands the network. It is incomplete. Campus Tees may blame the courier; the courier may see a late warehouse release.

**Main paper point:** one firm cannot fully control the network. Solving a problem may need changes in several relationships. Close links support learning, but can also create dependence.


# Negotiations

## Two types of negotiation

**Slides 3–6 and Larsson (2020).** Negotiation helps people reach a shared decision when their needs differ. A good negotiator finds the other side's needs and explains their own.

| Type | Lecture idea | Simple Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distributive | A fixed pie to divide: win–lose. | With all other terms fixed, a lower price gives the supplier less money. |
| Integrative | Expand the pie: win–win. | A steady order plan helps the supplier cut costs and offer better delivery. |

[diagram:negotiationpie]

A deal can include both types. First find a better way to work; then agree how to share the benefit.

## Prepare: objectives and BATNA

**Slides 8–9.** Gather facts, rank needs, set goals and understand the other side.

**Exact BATNA expansion:**

> best alternative to a negotiated agreement

**Plain English:** your best real option if you do not reach a deal.

**Campus Tees:** Supplier B can provide suitable blanks on time. Using B is the BATNA. A maximum acceptable price is a limit, not the alternative itself.

Set three outcomes: **worst acceptable, reasonable/fair, and best possible**. Compare total price, quality and delivery. Do not claim a backup exists if it does not.

## Seven negotiation phases

**Slide 7 and slides 10–15.**

| Phase | Main task | Campus Tees example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preparations | Gather facts and set goals. | Check price, stock and backup supply. |
| Greeting | Build a useful working relationship. | Show interest and listen. |
| Introduction | Agree on the purpose and agenda. | List price, quantity and delivery issues. |
| Argumentation | Give reasons and understand needs. | Explain why Friday delivery matters. |
| Compromise | Trade issues in a complete package. | Offer steady volume for reliable weekly deliveries. |
| Closure | Write down the full agreement. | Confirm sizes, dates, price and responsibilities. |
| Realisation | Carry out and check the agreement. | Send the promised order plan and check deliveries. |

[diagram:phases]

**From Larsson's paper:** a signed deal is not the end. Realisation matters because the agreed work must happen. It also affects the next negotiation.

## Trade issues together

Campus Tees wants a good price and reliable supply. The supplier wants steady volume and fewer urgent changes. Agree on a package that links these needs.

Do not accept each demand separately. Check the whole offer. Stay calm, avoid ultimatums and never lie.

## Culture: ask rather than assume

**Slides 17–22:** culture can affect time, trust and how people reach an agreement. The slides contrast a Swedish focus on plans and contracts with a Chinese focus on relationships, face and reciprocity.

These are broad teaching patterns, not rules for every person. Ask what matters to this supplier. Listen, check that both sides understand, and show respect.


# Glossary

## 3PL – Third Party Logistics

3PL stands for third-party logistics. It means a business hires an outside company to handle part or all its supply chain operations, such as warehousing, inventory tracking, packing, shipping, and returns.

Plain English: Another firm does logistics work for you.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees pays a firm to store, pack and send shirts.

Note: The agreement decides which tasks it does.

## 4PL – Fourth Party Logistics

Fourth-party logistics (4PL) is a supply chain management model where a company outsources its entire end-to-end logistics network and strategy to a single external provider.

4PL has a high-level management focus, handling integration and oversight of the entire supply chain often including a 3PL.

Plain English: One firm plans and manages a wider logistics network.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees uses a partner to coordinate storage firms and carriers.

Note: The key role is coordination, not just transport.

## ABC classification

A common way to classify inventory is the ABC classification.

A items have a high value, often representing about 80% of the total inventory

B items have medium value

C items have low value

ABC classification is used to put effort to items that affect the result the most. It is connected to the Pareto criteria (80/20 rule) where 20% of you inventory items represent 80% of the cost.

Plain English: Spend more time managing items with high annual usage value.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees checks its high-value blank-shirt stock often.

Note: A cheap item can still stop work if it is missing.

## Agile supply chain management

Agile supply chain management focuses on flexibility and responsiveness to meet rapidly changing customer demands and market conditions. It also makes the process efficient and empowers the employees.

Plain English: Respond to changing demand with good information and flexible work.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees changes the print mix after clubs confirm their designs.

Note: Speed must still meet cost and quality needs.

## Business Process Reengineering (BPR)

Business Process Reengineering (BPR) is the radical redesign of core business workflows and processes to achieve dramatic improvements in productivity, cycle times, and quality

Plain English: Make a major change to a business process.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees replaces separate order forms with one shared order flow.

Note: Kaizen usually means smaller, ongoing improvements.

## EOQ – Economic Order Quantity

The Economic Order Quantity is the optimal number of items to order at a given time. The EOQ formula (sometime referred to as the Wilson formula) balances two costs. The cost of ordering inventory falls with the increase in ordering volume due to purchasing on economies of scale. However, as the size of inventory grows, the cost of holding the inventory rises. EOQ is the exact point that minimizes both of these inversely related costs, see appendix A for the formula and its variables. 

Plain English: Find the order size that balances ordering and holding costs.

Campus Tees: For D=12,000, K=€30 and h=€2, Campus Tees orders 600 blanks.

Note: The basic model assumes steady demand and a fixed unit price.

## ERP – Enterprise Resource Planning

Enterprise resource planning (ERP) is the integrated management of main business processes, often in real time and mediated by software and technology.

Plain English: Join data and processes across the business.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees links sales, purchasing and finance.

Note: The data must still be correct.

## JIT – Just In Time

Just-in-time (JIT) inventory management aims to increase efficiency and reduce costs by ordering products only on an as-needed basis. 

Plain English: Bring materials close to the time they are needed.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees gets reliable small deliveries of packing material.

Note: JIT needs reliable quality, information and suppliers.

## Kanban

Kanban is a just-in-time system in which new item orders are triggered automatically via cards or other signals.

Plain English: Use a signal to tell someone to refill used stock.

Campus Tees: An empty box tells the supplier to send more blanks.

Note: Set a suitable amount and refill time.

## Kaizen

Kaizen is a Japanese philosophy focusing on continuous improvement. 

Plain English: Keep making small improvements.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees improves its artwork checklist after an error.

Note: Check whether the change helps.

## FIFO – First In First Out

The oldest items in the inventory are sold first. Therefore, the cost of the oldest item should be used when calculating your cost of sold goods. Compare with LIFO.

Plain English: Use the oldest inventory cost first.

Campus Tees: Buy ten blanks at €2, then ten at €3. FIFO cost for ten sold is €20.

Note: The accounting rule and physical stock movement can differ.

## Lean supply chain management

Lean supply chain management focuses on waste reduction, inventory optimization and continuous improvement,

Plain English: Remove waste and keep work flowing.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees removes duplicate order entry and waiting.

Note: Do not remove a useful buffer without checking the effect.

## LIFO – Last In First Out

When using LIFO as an inventory valuation method it is assumed that the Last items in are sold First. An example of this could be companies that sell sand or gravel. Compare with FIFO.

Plain English: Use the newest inventory cost first.

Campus Tees: Buy ten blanks at €2, then ten at €3. LIFO cost for ten sold is €30.

Note: This explains the idea, not where accounting rules allow it.

## MPS – Master Production Schedule

A production plan that helps you to determine when to order and how to allocate production resources like personnel and machines. 

Plain English: Plan the finished output and its timing.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees plans to print 300 shirts next week.

Note: MRP then plans the materials needed.

## MRO = Maintenance, repair, and operating

MRO items are anything that is used to maintain, repair, and operate your inventory management system.

Plain English: Supplies used to keep the business running.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees buys cleaning fluid and printer spares.

Note: These support the work rather than form the main product.

## MRP – Material Requirements Planning

Material Requirements Planning is a system that helps businesses manage inventory by determining what materials are needed, in what quantities, and when they are required for production.

Plain English: Plan the materials, amounts and timing needed for output.

Campus Tees: A plan for 300 shirts uses stock data to find how many blanks to buy.

Note: Also check planned deliveries and lead times.

## MUDA – Waste

There are seven kinds of waste (MUDA), 1 Overproduction, 2 Defects, 3 Inventory, 4 Motion, 5 Over processing, 6 Transporting, 7 Waiting. 

Plain English: Find seven types of waste.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees finds waiting, wrong prints and extra box movements.

Note: Motion is people moving; transport is goods moving.

## QR – Quick Repsonse

Quick Response (QR) Code Inventory Management uses scannable optical labels to track stock levels, locations, and product details in real time.

Plain English: The source paragraph explains scanning QR codes to identify stock.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees scans a box when it arrives.

Note: The glossary heading uses QR differently from an agile quick-response strategy.

## RFID = Radio-frequency identification

Radio-frequency identification (RFID) is used in inventory management to track individual items within the system.

Plain English: Use radio tags to identify or track items.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees reads tagged shirt boxes at the warehouse.

Note: The recorded movement must still be correct.

## Safety Stock

A safety stock (often referred to as a buffer stock) is extra inventory held to protect against stockouts caused by demand fluctuations or supply delays.

Plain English: Keep extra stock against late supply or higher demand.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees holds 60 extra blank shirts.

Note: The amount depends on service needs and uncertainty.

## Six Sigma

Six Sigma is a data-driven methodology and set of techniques used to improve business processes by eliminating defects and reducing variability

Plain English: Use data to reduce defects and variation.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees measures wrong prints and checks their causes.

Note: Measure the result of each change.

## SKU – Stock Keeping Unit

A stock-keeping unit (SKU) is a code attached to items within your inventory often in form of a barcode, QR code or RFID tags. 

Plain English: Give each separately managed stock variant an ID.

Campus Tees: Small white and medium white shirts have different SKUs.

Note: Barcodes, QR codes and RFID can carry this ID.

## TQM – Total Quality Management

An organisation-wide effort to work with quality and continous improvement (Kaizen). Today often replaced by ISO9000, Six Sigma and Lean manufacturing.

Plain English: Make quality a responsibility across the whole business.

Campus Tees: Sales and printing work together to prevent wrong logos.

Note: TQM, lean and Six Sigma can be used together.

## VMI = Vendor-managed inventory

Vendor-managed inventory (VMI) is inventory that is monitored and replenished by the vendor itself—rather than the business owner.

Plain English: The supplier checks stock and refills it under agreed rules.

Campus Tees: The packing supplier checks use and refills Campus Tees’ boxes.

Note: VMI does not by itself decide who owns the stock.

## WMS – Warehouse Management System

A WMS helps a business to manage day-to-day operations within their warehouse. 

Plain English: Manage daily warehouse tasks and stock locations.

Campus Tees: Campus Tees uses a WMS to receive, find, pick and send shirts.

Note: ERP joins wider business data; MRP plans materials.

# New practice papers

These are new study questions written in the style of the supplied exams. Each paper has two 5-point and two 10-point questions. They do not repeat the supplied past questions. Answers and checklists are study help, not official marking schemes.

# Practice paper 1

## Question 1 — 5 points

Shortly describe the difference between needs, wants and demands. Give one example of each from Campus Tees.

Study answer:

A need is a state of felt deprivation. A want is the form a need takes through culture and personality. Demand means wants backed by purchasing power.

A student club needs its team to feel united. It wants orange shirts with its logo. When it has a budget and can pay for 100 shirts, this becomes demand. The three terms show different steps; they are not three names for buying a shirt.

## Question 2 — 5 points

Shortly describe fixed and variable costs. Give one example of each and explain why fixed costs can increase.

Study answer:

Fixed costs stay the same within a given output range and period. Variable costs change with output. Campus Tees pays the same monthly room rent when it prints 100 or 200 shirts. Buying more blank shirts raises its material cost.

Fixed does not mean unchanged forever. If the firm needs another room, rent can rise to a new fixed level. State the time period and output range when explaining the cost.

## Question 3 — 10 points

Describe and exemplify how lean and agile methods can be combined in a printing company. Discuss where the customer order decoupling point should be placed.

Study answer:

Lean removes waste and supports steady work. Agile uses good market information and flexible resources to respond to change. Leagile combines them in one chain.

Campus Tees can buy common blank shirts in steady batches. It waits for the club to confirm the design before printing. The customer order decoupling point is where the product becomes linked to that order. Holding common blanks before printing supports this choice.

This can reduce unsold printed designs while keeping delivery quick. However, the printer still needs to predict total demand and sizes. It also needs enough printing time and capacity after the order arrives. If finishing takes longer than the customer will wait, the plan must change.

## Question 4 — 10 points

Describe and discuss how Campus Tees should prepare for a supplier negotiation. Use BATNA and give two examples of issues that could be negotiated together.

Study answer:

Campus Tees should check demand, prices, quality needs, delivery dates and available suppliers. It should rank its needs and set its worst acceptable, fair and best possible outcomes.

BATNA means best alternative to a negotiated agreement. A qualified second supplier that can deliver on time is a real alternative. A maximum price is a limit, not the BATNA itself.

First, Campus Tees could offer steady order volume in return for a lower price. Second, it could give earlier order information in return for reliable weekly deliveries. These packages may help both sides. The firm should compare the complete offer with its alternative, then write down the agreed terms and responsibilities.

# Practice paper 2

## Question 1 — 5 points

Shortly describe the four stages of supply chain integration. Illustrate the final stage with one example.

Study answer:

At the baseline stage, departments mainly work separately. Functional integration joins related tasks into functions. Internal integration joins work across the firm. External integration connects the firm with suppliers and customers.

For example, Campus Tees shares confirmed club orders with its wholesaler. Both firms use the same delivery plan. This helps purchasing, printing and supply support the final deadline rather than follow separate plans.

## Question 2 — 5 points

Describe and exemplify the difference between TQM and BPR.

Study answer:

TQM is a firm-wide effort to improve quality and keep improving. BPR means business process reengineering: a major redesign of a process.

Campus Tees can use TQM by having sales and printing check why wrong logos occur and improve their daily routine. BPR could replace a slow paper-based order process with a new shared order flow. Both may improve results, but they differ in the size and type of change.

## Question 3 — 10 points

Use Barney's resource-based view to discuss whether Campus Tees can keep an advantage over other printers. Apply the VRIN tests to a shared supplier routine.

Study answer:

The resource-based view looks at how a firm uses resources such as equipment, skills, knowledge and routines. Barney asks when these differences can support a sustained advantage.

A shared routine that helps Campus Tees meet event deadlines is valuable if clubs care about reliable delivery. It is rare if few rivals have an equal routine. It may be hard to copy because it depends on years of trust and shared learning. It is non-substitutable only if rivals cannot gain the same benefit through another available method.

The routine must pass all four tests. A standard printer that anyone can buy is less likely to do so. Even a strong routine can lose value if club needs change. Sustained advantage does not mean that success lasts forever.

## Question 4 — 10 points

Campus Tees uses 18,000 blanks per year over 300 working days. Ordering costs €40 per order and holding costs €4 per unit per year. Lead time is 4 working days and safety stock is 60. Calculate EOQ and reorder point. Explain their different purposes and state two assumptions.

Study answer:

EOQ = √(2DK/h) = √(2 × 18,000 × 40 / 4) = √360,000 = 600 blanks per order.

Daily demand = 18,000 / 300 = 60 blanks. ROP = daily demand × lead time + safety stock = 60 × 4 + 60 = 300 blanks.

EOQ sets the order size. ROP sets the point at which the firm starts a new order. At this EOQ, there are 30 orders per year and 300 units of average cycle stock. Annual ordering and cycle-stock holding costs are €1,200 each.

The basic EOQ model assumes steady demand and a fixed unit price. It also assumes known lead time and complete deliveries. Daily demand and lead time must use matching time units.

# Practice paper 3

## Question 1 — 5 points

Shortly describe a network picture. Give one example showing why two firms may understand the same supply problem differently.

Study answer:

A network picture is an actor's understanding of its business network. It is incomplete because the actor does not know every link or cause.

Campus Tees may think late shirts are caused by a slow courier. The courier may know that the wholesaler released the boxes late. Their different views can lead to different actions. Comparing information can help them find the cause and agree on a useful change.

## Question 2 — 5 points

Shortly describe ERP and MRP. Explain how their roles differ in Campus Tees.

Study answer:

ERP means Enterprise Resource Planning. It joins data and processes across the business. MRP means Material Requirements Planning. It works out the materials, amounts and timing needed for planned output.

Campus Tees can use ERP to connect sales, purchasing and finance. For an order of 300 shirts, MRP checks stock and planned receipts to find how many extra blanks are needed and when. The roles can be linked inside one system, but they are not the same task.

## Question 3 — 10 points

Describe and exemplify the main benefits and hidden costs of outsourcing. Discuss whether Campus Tees should keep its printing work inside the business.

Study answer:

Outsourcing transfers a business process to an independent outside firm. It can provide skills, lower costs and free resources for core work. Campus Tees could use a specialist for a print method it cannot offer itself.

The invoice is not the full cost. Hidden costs include defects, checking the supplier, sharing information and setting up the new work process. Late changes may also need extra coordination. The firm may become dependent on the supplier or lose useful skills.

Campus Tees should keep printing inside if that skill is central to its customer promise and hard to replace. It may buy specialist work outside if the supplier adds real value. The decision should compare quality, delivery, skills and total cost, rather than choose the lowest price alone.

## Question 4 — 10 points

Describe how Campus Tees can reduce waiting time and defects in an order process. Give two improvements and discuss one cost or limit of each.

Study answer:

First, Campus Tees can map the time spent on work and waiting. If orders wait for artwork, a clear approval deadline and shared order status can reduce delay. However, staff must keep the data correct, and customers must approve the design on time.

Second, it can check size and logo details before a full print run. A small trial can find errors early and reduce rework. The check takes time and uses a sample, so it should focus on errors that matter.

A cause-and-effect diagram can help list possible causes under people, machines, materials and methods. The firm should check these ideas with evidence. It can then compare waiting time, wrong prints and delivery results. Removing all checks may look faster but can lead to more defects.
